nodes.title: Incident response: Key Ideas
nodes.content: IR follows a documented lifecycle so a panicked 3am pager doesn't turn into 'what do we do now?'. The classic NIST flow is preparation, detection, containment, eradication, recovery, lessons learned. Exam questions test which phase owns which action.

flashcards.front: NIST IR lifecycle — name the phases.
flashcards.back: (1) Preparation: playbooks, contact lists, hardened images. (2) Detection & Analysis: SIEM alerts, IDS, user reports. (3) Containment: short-term (isolate host) + long-term (block C2 domains). (4) Eradication: remove malware, close vuln. (5) Recovery: restore from clean backup, monitor for re-infection. (6) Lessons learned: post-mortem within 2 weeks, action items tracked.

Short-term: stop the bleed fast — pull the network cable, kill the user session, block the IP. May be reversible. Long-term: durable fix — patch the vuln, rotate creds, deploy IPS rule, sometimes rebuild from scratch. Don't skip short-term: every minute of attacker dwell time multiplies damage.

flashcards.front: Chain of custody — why does it matter?
flashcards.back: If the incident leads to prosecution, evidence must be admissible — every transfer, image, and access logged from acquisition to court. Drives required to be hashed (SHA-256) immediately, copies (not originals) used for analysis, originals stored in a tamper-evident bag with signatures. Skip this and the lawyer dismisses your case.

flashcards.front: What's a post-mortem (lessons learned) supposed to produce?
flashcards.back: Blameless write-up within 2 weeks: timeline, what worked, what didn't, action items with owners + due dates. The goal is process improvement, not punishment — if engineers fear blame they hide details and the next incident is worse. Track action items in your normal sprint board, not in a doc nobody reopens.

nodes.title: Microsoft Defender for Cloud (AZ-500): Key Ideas
nodes.content: Defender for Cloud (formerly Azure Security Center + Azure Defender) is the primary security posture management and workload protection service on Azure. AZ-500 tests Secure Score interpretation, which workload protection plans to enable, regulatory compliance mapping, and the distinction between Defender for Cloud and Defender for Endpoint.

flashcards.front: What is Secure Score and how do you raise it?
flashcards.back: Secure Score is a percentage summarizing how well your Azure environment follows security recommendations — each recommendation is worth a defined number of points. To raise it: remediate recommendations, enable MFA, apply missing OS patches, restrict public network access, enable logging. It is not a compliance score — it measures posture, not a specific standard.

flashcards.front: Defender for Cloud workload protection plans — name three and their targets.
flashcards.back: Defender for Servers: agent-based threat detection, vulnerability assessment, adaptive application controls for VMs. Defender for SQL: anomaly detection and vulnerability scans for Azure SQL / SQL Server on VMs. Defender for Containers: runtime threat detection, image scanning, and hardening for AKS and container registries. Each plan is enabled per subscription and has its own per-resource cost.

flashcards.front: Regulatory compliance in Defender for Cloud — what does it do?
flashcards.back: Maps Azure resource configurations to specific controls in frameworks such as PCI DSS, ISO 27001, NIST SP 800-53, and the Microsoft Cloud Security Benchmark. The dashboard shows passing vs failing controls per standard. It does not certify compliance — it shows your current posture against the standard's control requirements so you know what to remediate before an audit.

flashcards.front: Microsoft Defender for Cloud (MDfC) vs Microsoft Defender for Endpoint (MDfE) — key distinction.
flashcards.back: MDfC is an Azure-native service that monitors cloud resource configurations, detects threats across Azure workloads, and manages security recommendations across subscriptions — cloud security posture management (CSPM) + cloud workload protection (CWPP). MDfE is an endpoint detection and response (EDR) agent installed on Windows/macOS/Linux devices that detects malware, behavioral anomalies, and provides threat hunting. MDfC can integrate MDfE data but they serve different scopes.

nodes.title: Mixed exam topics: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Some exam objectives don't fit neatly into a single domain — they span protocols, tools, or concepts covered briefly in multiple sections. These cards treat each item as a stand-alone fact, the way an exam question presents it: one concept, one answer.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between a hub, a switch, and a router?
flashcards.back: Hub: Layer 1, repeats every frame to all ports — all devices share bandwidth, collisions guaranteed. Switch: Layer 2, forwards frames using a MAC address table to only the destination port — full duplex, no collisions, each port gets full bandwidth. Router: Layer 3, makes forwarding decisions based on IP address, connects different networks. Hub is legacy; switches dominate LAN; routers are at network edges.

flashcards.front: What is RAID 5 and how many drives can it tolerate losing?
flashcards.back: RAID 5 stripes data and parity across at least 3 drives. Any single drive failure can be recovered by reconstructing missing data from the remaining drives and parity. It cannot tolerate 2 simultaneous drive failures. Effective capacity = (N-1) × drive size. Read performance is excellent; write requires parity recalculation. RAID 6 tolerates 2 failures using double parity.

flashcards.front: What does a proxy server do, and how does a forward proxy differ from a reverse proxy?
flashcards.back: Forward proxy: sits between clients and the internet on behalf of clients — used for content filtering, caching, and anonymizing outbound requests (the server sees the proxy's IP). Reverse proxy: sits in front of servers on behalf of the server — used for load balancing, SSL termination, caching, and hiding backend topology (the client sees the proxy's IP). Both intermediate HTTP, but they protect opposite sides.

flashcards.front: What is the purpose of a DMZ in network architecture?
flashcards.back: A demilitarized zone is a network segment between the untrusted internet and the trusted internal network, typically protected by two firewalls (or two interfaces on one firewall). Public-facing services (web, email, DNS) sit in the DMZ: internet can reach them but not the internal network; if the DMZ host is compromised, the inner firewall still blocks access to the internal LAN.
